summary: Carney concludes free-trade talks with the Philippines and says a US deal is possible but not there yet, while Ontario moves to tighten OSAP at private colleges.
body: In Manila for the ASEAN summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. concluded free-trade negotiations; formal signing is expected in 2027.[^1] Ottawa says the deal could triple Canadian exports to the Philippines by 2035, and talks with the ASEAN bloc as a whole are essentially finished too.[^1][^2] On the United States, Carney said after a long call with President Trump: "We are making progress... But we're not yet there," adding that Canada will not accept terms that hurt its auto industry.[^2]

On Brampton, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Ottawa and Ontario have offered Stellantis an "aggressive package" to stop the sale of its idle plant to Roshel, and will pitch the carmaker's global CEO together with Unifor.[^3] The two sides still disagree on how much subsidy money Stellantis must return; CBC confirmed Ottawa paid the company $222 million in 2023-25.[^3] CTV reports lobby records showing aides to Joly and to the prime minister met Roshel before the sale was announced, which Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says shows the government was involved.[^4]

Closer to home for students: Ontario will table a bill on Nov 16 to tighten OSAP, the province's student aid, at private career colleges. It would cap OSAP-funded growth, make mostly online programs ineligible and make schools liable for students' loans, after an audit found courses finished in a day and thousands of applications from the same internet addresses.[^5] One GTA college's OSAP users rose from 562 to 17,157 in three years.[^6] The NDP and Liberals say the bill comes too late.[^5][^6]
differences: Joly says Stellantis still owes "hundreds of millions" in subsidies; the company has offered to return far less.[^3] Poilievre says lobby records show the government was involved in the Roshel sale.[^4]

reads.title: Ontario proposes OSAP changes after 'systematic and widespread' problems at private career colleges
